editions.name: No. 14 chair
editions.note: Six pieces of steam-bent beech, ten screws and two nuts. Shipped flat by the millions, it became the café chair.

editions.name: Morris chair
editions.note: One of the first reclining armchairs: a pegged bar at the back sets the angle.

editions.name: Sitzmaschine
editions.note: A "machine for sitting". The back reclines onto a row of wooden knobs on each side.

editions.name: Hill House ladder-back chair
editions.note: Made for a bedroom at the Hill House, more a piece of the room's design than a chair to sit in.

editions.name: Calvet chair
editions.note: Carved for the offices of Casa Calvet in Barcelona. The oak curves around the body like bone.

editions.name: Red and Blue Chair
editions.note: Boards and rails held apart so you can see how it's made. Rietveld painted it in primary colors around 1923.

editions.name: Zig-Zag chair
editions.note: Four flat boards folded into a Z. No legs at all.

editions.name: Wassily Chair
editions.note: Breuer took the idea from his bicycle's handlebars: bent steel tube and taut leather, made at the Bauhaus.

editions.name: Cesca chair
editions.note: A cantilever with no back legs, so it gives a little when you sit. Named after Breuer's daughter Francesca.

editions.name: Barcelona chair
editions.by: Ludwig Mies van der Rohe and Lilly Reich
editions.note: Made for the German Pavilion at the 1929 Barcelona exhibition, as seating fit for the King and Queen of Spain.

editions.name: Brno chair
editions.by: Ludwig Mies van der Rohe and Lilly Reich
editions.note: Designed for Villa Tugendhat in Brno. A single steel bar bent into a C on each side.

editions.name: LC4 chaise longue
editions.by: Le Corbusier, Pierre Jeanneret and Charlotte Perriand
editions.note: Le Corbusier called it a relaxing machine. The curved frame slides on its base from upright to almost flat.

editions.name: LC2 armchair
editions.by: Le Corbusier, Pierre Jeanneret and Charlotte Perriand
editions.note: Cushions held in a steel cage: the frame sits on the outside, the opposite of a club chair.

editions.name: Paimio Chair
editions.note: Made for Aalto's tuberculosis sanatorium in Paimio. The angle of the back was meant to help patients breathe.

editions.name: Stool 60
editions.note: Three bent birch legs on a round seat. They stack into a spiral, and millions have been made since 1933.

editions.name: Tolix A chair
editions.note: Galvanized sheet steel, made to stand outside French cafés and stack high.

editions.name: Landi Chair
editions.note: Made for the 1939 Swiss National Exhibition, the Landi. One pressed aluminum shell punched full of holes.

editions.name: Butterfly chair (BKF)
editions.by: Antonio Bonet, Juan Kurchan and Jorge Ferrari Hardoy
editions.note: Three architects in Buenos Aires, one bent steel rod and a leather sling. One of the most copied chairs ever.

editions.name: Navy chair (1006)
editions.note: Made for warships out of recycled aluminum, welded and heat-treated by hand. It's meant to last 150 years.

editions.name: LCW
editions.note: Molded plywood joined by rubber shock mounts. Time magazine called it the chair of the century.

editions.name: La Chaise
editions.note: Made for a MoMA competition after Gaston Lachaise's sculpture Floating Figure. Not produced until 1990.

editions.name: Eames Plastic Armchair
editions.note: One of the first mass-produced plastic chairs. The same shell came on wire, wood or rocker bases.

editions.name: Womb Chair
editions.note: Florence Knoll asked Saarinen for a chair she could curl up in, like a basket full of pillows.

editions.name: Tulip chair
editions.note: Saarinen wanted to clear up "the slum of legs" under tables, so chair and table got one stem each.

editions.name: Diamond chair
editions.note: Bertoia was a sculptor. He said these chairs are mostly made of air, and space passes right through them.

editions.name: Coconut Chair
editions.note: Shaped like a wedge of coconut shell. It looks light, but the first ones had a heavy steel shell.

editions.name: Ant chair
editions.note: One sheet of molded plywood pinched at the waist, on three legs at first. Made for a pharmaceutical company's canteen.

editions.name: Series 7 chair
editions.note: The Ant's four-legged sibling, and one of the best-selling chairs ever made.

editions.name: Egg chair
editions.note: Made for the SAS Royal Hotel in Copenhagen, which Jacobsen designed down to the door handles and cutlery.

editions.name: Swan chair
editions.note: Also for the SAS Royal Hotel. There isn't a straight line anywhere on it.

editions.name: Wishbone Chair
editions.note: Inspired by portraits of Danish merchants sitting in Ming dynasty chairs. The Y-shaped back gave it its name.

editions.name: The Chair
editions.note: Kennedy and Nixon sat in it for the first televised US presidential debate, in 1960.

editions.name: Papa Bear chair
editions.note: Big wings and padded wooden paws at the ends of the arms. It hugs you back.

editions.name: Shell Chair
editions.note: Three legs and a seat that seems to float. It flopped in 1963 and wasn't made again until the late 1990s.

editions.name: PK24
editions.note: A long curve of woven cane on a steel frame. The seat slides in its base to change the angle.

editions.name: Spanish Chair
editions.note: Inspired by low leather chairs Mogensen saw in Spain. The wide flat arms hold a glass.

editions.name: Chieftain Chair
editions.note: Sculpted teak arms and a seat that floats inside the frame. King Frederik IX tried it at its 1949 debut.

editions.name: Hanging Egg Chair
editions.note: A rattan egg hung from the ceiling, made so sitting would feel like being held.

editions.name: Ball Chair
editions.note: Aarnio needed a big chair for his new house and built one he could sit inside. A room within a room.

editions.name: Bubble Chair
editions.note: The Ball Chair made clear and hung from the ceiling, so light comes in from everywhere.

editions.name: Pastil chair
editions.note: A rocking chair shaped like a candy. It floats, so it works in the pool too.

editions.name: Karuselli
editions.note: Kukkapuro is said to have found its shape by sitting in a snowdrift. It spins and rocks on a steel spring.

editions.name: Panton Chair
editions.note: The first chair molded from a single piece of plastic: one S-shaped curve, no legs, no joints.

editions.name: Cone Chair
editions.note: A cone balanced on its point. Made first for his parents' restaurant on the island of Funen.

editions.name: Superleggera
editions.note: "Super light", about 1.7 kg. Ponti threw it out of a fourth-floor window to show it wouldn't break.

editions.name: Mezzadro
editions.note: A tractor seat on a sprung steel bar with a beech foot. A ready-made, in the spirit of Duchamp.

editions.name: Tube Chair
editions.note: Four padded tubes of different sizes, sold nested in a bag, that clip together into a chair any way you like.

editions.name: Plia
editions.note: A folding chair that folds almost flat around a three-disc hinge. Millions sold.

editions.name: Sacco
editions.by: Piero Gatti, Cesare Paolini and Franco Teodoro
editions.note: A bag of polystyrene beads that takes your shape. The first designer bean bag.

editions.name: Up 5 (La Mamma)
editions.note: Sold vacuum-packed flat, it swelled to full size when unwrapped. Its ball-shaped footstool is chained to it.

editions.name: Joe
editions.by: Jonathan De Pas, Donato D'Urbino and Paolo Lomazzi
editions.note: A giant baseball glove you sit in, named for Joe DiMaggio.

editions.name: Djinn chair
editions.note: Low and wavy. It's the red seating in the space station in Kubrick's 2001: A Space Odyssey.

editions.name: Ribbon chair
editions.note: A ribbon of stretch fabric folded over itself on a lacquered base.

editions.name: Polypropylene chair
editions.note: Tens of millions made. The stacking chair of British schools, halls and churches.

editions.name: Wiggle Side Chair
editions.note: Layers of corrugated cardboard glued in alternating directions, strong enough to stand on.

editions.name: Proust armchair
editions.note: A fake antique armchair painted all over in dots borrowed from a Paul Signac painting.

editions.name: First chair
editions.note: Memphis in one chair: a hoop, two balls for arms and a disc for a back.

editions.name: How High the Moon
editions.note: A big club armchair made of nothing but steel mesh. You can see straight through it.

editions.name: Miss Blanche
editions.note: Paper roses floating in clear acrylic, inspired by Blanche DuBois's dress in A Streetcar Named Desire.

editions.name: Well Tempered Chair
editions.note: Four sheets of tempered steel rolled and bolted into an armchair. It bounces when you sit.

editions.name: Lockheed Lounge
editions.note: Riveted aluminum over a fiberglass body. One sold for £2.4 million, a record for a living designer at the time.

editions.name: Knotted Chair
editions.note: Macramé from aramid and carbon rope, soaked in epoxy and hung to harden. Gravity gave it its shape.

editions.name: Vermelha chair
editions.note: Hundreds of meters of red rope wound by hand over a steel frame. Every one comes out different.

editions.name: Air-Chair
editions.note: Gas is injected into the mold so the chair comes out hollow, light and in one shot.

editions.name: Louis Ghost
editions.note: A Louis XVI armchair in clear polycarbonate, molded in one piece.

editions.name: Chair One
editions.note: Flat aluminum faces joined like a soccer ball, on a concrete base.

editions.name: Vegetal
editions.note: Grown like a plant: branches spread from four stems and weave into a seat.

editions.name: Spun chair
editions.note: A spinning top you sit in. Lean back and it rotates all the way round.

editions.name: Aeron chair
editions.note: No foam: a stretched mesh seat and back that let air through.

editions.name: Adirondack chair
editions.note: Thomas Lee built it from a handful of flat boards on vacation in Westport, New York. Wide arms, made for a drink.

editions.name: Windsor chair
editions.note: Spindles socketed into a solid wooden seat, no upholstery. Made by English chairmakers since the early 1700s.

editions.name: Shaker chair
editions.note: The Shakers believed beauty comes from usefulness. Their chairs are light enough to hang on a peg rail.

editions.name: Monobloc chair
editions.note: Injection-molded in under a minute. Probably the most common chair on Earth.

editions.name: Acapulco chair
editions.note: Vinyl cord woven over an oval steel frame. Nobody knows who designed it.

editions.name: Butaque
editions.note: Porset reworked the butaque, a low reclining chair with colonial roots, into a modern classic.

editions.name: Office cane chair
editions.note: Made locally for the offices of Chandigarh, the new city Le Corbusier and Jeanneret planned. The V legs became its signature.

editions.name: Standard chair
editions.note: The back legs are thick because that's where the weight goes when you lean back. Prouvé built furniture like an engineer.

editions.name: Ming horseshoe armchair
editions.note: Held together by joinery alone. Chairs like this inspired Wegner's Wishbone and The Chair.

editions.name: Butterfly Stool
editions.note: Two identical curves of molded plywood held together by a single brass rod.

editions.name: Tiffany lamp
editions.note: Hundreds of pieces of colored glass set in copper foil. Many of the famous designs were Clara Driscoll's, credited only a century later.

editions.name: Lampe Gras
editions.note: A factory and office lamp with no screws or welds in the arm. Le Corbusier used them in his studio.

editions.name: Wagenfeld lamp
editions.by: Wilhelm Wagenfeld and Carl Jakob Jucker
editions.note: The Bauhaus lamp: glass base, glass stem, opal glass dome. Made in the school's metal workshop.

editions.name: Anglepoise lamp
editions.note: Carwardine was a car engineer. Springs balance the arm the way muscles hold a limb, so it stays where you leave it.

editions.name: Akari lamps
editions.note: Noguchi went to Gifu, famous for paper lanterns, and remade them in mulberry paper and bamboo. Akari means light.

editions.name: PH5
editions.note: Shades arranged so you never see the bulb, only soft reflected light. Henningsen spent decades fighting glare.

editions.name: PH Artichoke
editions.note: Made for the Langelinie Pavilion in Copenhagen: 72 copper leaves in 12 rows, each one hiding the light.

editions.name: Arco
editions.note: A ceiling light with no ceiling. The marble base has a hole so two people can carry it on a broom handle.

editions.name: Pipistrello
editions.note: "Bat" in Italian, for the scalloped shade. Designed for the Olivetti showroom in Paris.

editions.name: Eclisse
editions.note: A lamp with its own eclipse: turn the inner shell to dim it from full to a sliver.

editions.name: Nesso
editions.note: A molded plastic mushroom from a competition run by the magazine Domus and Artemide.

editions.name: Flowerpot
editions.note: Two half spheres facing each other, named for the flower power years.

editions.name: Tizio
editions.note: Counterweights instead of springs, and the arms carry the current, so no wires. Sapper wanted a lamp for working late.

editions.name: Atollo
editions.note: A cylinder, a cone and a half sphere. Geometry you'd draw as a kid, turned into a lamp.

editions.name: Ashoka
editions.note: A Memphis table lamp of thin colored arms and bare bulbs, named after the Indian emperor.

editions.name: Tolomeo
editions.by: Michele De Lucchi and Giancarlo Fassina
editions.note: A task lamp with fishing-line cables instead of exposed springs. One of the best-selling lamps ever.

editions.name: Taccia
editions.note: A glass bowl resting loose on a fluted column, like a classical capital. Tilt the bowl to aim the light.

editions.name: Parentesi
editions.note: A steel tube bent like a bracket, slung on a cable from ceiling to floor. The light slides up and down it.

editions.name: Kaiser Idell 6556
editions.note: Dell ran the Bauhaus metal workshop before designing lamps for Kaiser. This desk lamp sold for decades.

editions.name: Jieldé lamp
editions.note: A mechanic tired of lamps breaking in his workshop made one with no wires in the joints. The name is his initials, JLD.

editions.name: Porca Miseria!
editions.note: A chandelier of smashed plates and cups, frozen mid-explosion. The name is an Italian curse.

editions.name: 85 Lamps
editions.note: Eighty-five bare bulbs and their cords bundled into a chandelier. One of Droog's first pieces.

editions.name: Lucellino
editions.note: A bare bulb with goose-feather wings. The name means little bird of light.

editions.name: Bourgie
editions.note: A baroque table lamp in clear plastic, a joke on bourgeois taste that became a bestseller.

editions.name: Noguchi table
editions.note: Two identical pieces of wood lock together under a heavy slab of glass. A sculptor's coffee table.

editions.name: Marshmallow sofa
editions.note: Eighteen round cushions floating on a steel frame. Pop furniture before Pop had a name.

editions.name: Eames Storage Unit
editions.note: Shelving built like the Eames House: a steel frame filled with colored panels.

editions.name: String shelf
editions.note: Won a competition for an affordable bookshelf. Wire ladders on the wall and thin shelves between.

editions.name: 606 Universal Shelving System
editions.note: Aluminum tracks on the wall and shelves you can move wherever you need them. Made since 1960.

editions.name: USM Haller
editions.note: Chrome balls and tubes in a grid with colored panels between. It started as office furniture for USM's own factory.

editions.name: Componibili
editions.note: Round plastic storage modules that stack. In production since 1967.

editions.name: Boby trolley
editions.note: A rolling tower of trays and swivel drawers, made for designers' tools.

editions.name: Camaleonda
editions.note: A sofa of tufted blocks you hook together with rings and straps into any shape.

editions.name: Togo
editions.note: All foam, no frame. Ducaroy compared it to a tube of toothpaste folded over on itself.

editions.name: Carlton bookcase
editions.note: The Memphis manifesto: a room divider of angled shelves in loud laminate. It barely holds books, and that's the point.

editions.name: Adjustable table E 1027
editions.note: Made for her villa E-1027 so her sister could have breakfast in bed. The base slides under the bed.

editions.name: Tea Trolley 900
editions.note: Bent birch loops, big white wheels and tiled shelves.

editions.name: Conoid Chair
editions.note: A walnut seat cantilevered off two long runners, with a spindle back. Nakashima said he gave trees a second life.

editions.name: Bookworm
editions.note: A flexible strip you bend into any curve on the wall. The books hold it in place.

editions.name: Polder sofa
editions.note: Long and low like the flat Dutch landscape, with cushions in several colors and big wooden buttons.

editions.name: Tansu chest
editions.note: Edo period chests with iron fittings and stepped drawers. Some had wheels, to roll them out of a burning house.

editions.name: Chesterfield sofa
editions.note: Deep-buttoned leather, arms as high as the back. The gentlemen's club sofa.

editions.name: Fallingwater
editions.note: Wright put the house over the waterfall instead of facing it. Its terraces cantilever out over the stream.

editions.name: Villa Savoye
editions.note: Le Corbusier's five points in one house: pillars, roof garden, open plan, ribbon windows, free facade.

editions.name: Farnsworth House
editions.note: A glass box floating over a floodplain. The client, Dr. Edith Farnsworth, sued Mies over the costs.

editions.name: Glass House
editions.note: The only room with walls is a brick cylinder holding the bathroom. Johnson lived there until he died in 2005.

editions.name: Eames House
editions.note: Case Study House No. 8, built from off-the-shelf factory parts. Charles and Ray lived there the rest of their lives.

editions.name: Stahl House
editions.note: Case Study House No. 22, cantilevered over the Hollywood Hills. Julius Shulman's night photo made it famous.

editions.name: Kaufmann Desert House
editions.note: Built for the same family as Fallingwater. The glass walls slide open and the wings pinwheel out into the desert.

editions.name: Rietveld Schröder House
editions.note: The upstairs walls slide away, turning separate rooms into one open space. A De Stijl painting you can live in.

editions.name: Villa Tugendhat
editions.note: The huge living room windows sink into the floor at the push of a button. One wall is a single slab of onyx.

editions.name: Villa Mairea
editions.note: Columns wrapped in rattan and poles placed like a forest. Aalto's clients let him experiment.

editions.name: E-1027
editions.note: Gray's house by the sea. Le Corbusier later painted murals on its walls without her permission.

editions.name: Maison de Verre
editions.note: A wall of glass blocks that glows like a lantern, slipped under the top floor because the tenant there refused to leave.

editions.name: Casa Barragán
editions.note: Plain from the street, full of color and light inside. Barragán lived there until he died in 1988.

editions.name: Cuadra San Cristóbal
editions.note: A horse ranch of pink and purple walls around a pool where the horses drink.

editions.name: Casa de Vidro
editions.note: Bo Bardi's own glass house on thin columns. The forest has grown up all around it.

editions.name: Curutchet House
editions.note: Le Corbusier's only house in the Americas, built for a surgeon. A tree grows up through the middle.

editions.name: Casa sobre el Arroyo
editions.note: A house that is a bridge: one concrete arch over a stream with the rooms on top. Built for the architect's father, the composer Alberto Williams.

editions.name: House NA
editions.note: A see-through house of 21 floor levels at different heights. Like living in a tree.

editions.name: Row House in Sumiyoshi
editions.note: A concrete box squeezed between old wooden row houses. To get from room to room you cross an open courtyard, rain or shine.

editions.name: Katsura Imperial Villa
editions.note: Modular rooms, sliding screens and no ornament. Modernists like Bruno Taut saw their own ideas here, 300 years early.

editions.name: Villa La Rotonda
editions.note: Four identical temple fronts, one on each side, so every view of the hills is the best one. Copied around the world.

editions.name: Casa Batlló
editions.note: The roof is a dragon's back, the balconies look like masks and the facade glitters with broken tile.

editions.name: The Hill House
editions.note: Mackintosh designed it all, walls to furniture. It soaked up so much rain it now sits inside a giant mesh box to dry out.

editions.name: Red House
editions.note: Built for William Morris and his new wife. Plain red brick with no stucco, which was radical then.

editions.name: Gamble House
editions.note: Every joint and peg shaped by hand, with deep Japanese-style eaves.

editions.name: Robie House
editions.note: Long and low like the prairie, with roofs that cantilever far past the walls.

editions.name: Gehry Residence
editions.note: Gehry wrapped an ordinary pink bungalow in chain-link and corrugated metal. The neighbors were not happy.

editions.name: Vanna Venturi House
editions.note: A house for the architect's mother and one of the first postmodern buildings: a split gable that says "house" like a child's drawing.

editions.name: Maison à Bordeaux
editions.note: For a man in a wheelchair: a whole room is an elevator platform that moves between the three floors.

editions.name: Sheats–Goldstein Residence
editions.note: A concrete cave in the hills, its coffered roof studded with drinking glasses that work as skylights.

editions.name: Chemosphere
editions.note: An octagon on a single concrete column on a steep hillside, reached by a funicular.

editions.name: Palais Bulles
editions.note: A cluster of rust-red bubbles on the cliffs over the Mediterranean, later Pierre Cardin's.

editions.name: Futuro House
editions.note: A prefab flying-saucer ski cabin that could be set down anywhere. Fewer than a hundred were made.

editions.name: Villa Müller
editions.note: A plain white cube outside. Inside, rooms at different levels flow into each other, what Loos called the Raumplan.

editions.name: Melnikov House
editions.note: Two interlocking cylinders pierced by dozens of hexagonal windows. A private house in Soviet Moscow.

editions.name: Rose Seidler House
editions.note: Built for the architect's parents. People came from all over Sydney to stare at it.

editions.name: Villa Shodhan
editions.note: A concrete parasol of a roof over a stack of rooms and terraces, built for Indian heat.

editions.name: Casa Malaparte
editions.note: A red box on a rock over the sea, with a roof that's a giant stair. Godard shot Le Mépris there.

editions.name: La Fábrica
editions.note: An old cement factory Bofill turned into his home and studio, now covered in ivy and eucalyptus.

editions.name: Villa Majorelle
editions.note: A painter's studio in a blue so strong it took his name: Majorelle blue. Yves Saint Laurent later bought it.

editions.name: Diego Rivera and Frida Kahlo House-Studio
editions.note: Two houses, a red one for him and a blue one for her, joined by a bridge at the roof.

editions.name: Great Pyramid of Giza
editions.note: The tallest structure people had built for about 3,800 years.
editions.credit: Douwe C. van der Zee · CC BY-SA 4.0

editions.name: Pantheon
editions.note: Nearly 1,900 years old, its dome is still the world's largest made of unreinforced concrete. The open eye at the top lets the rain in.

editions.name: Al-Khazneh
editions.note: Not built but carved: the whole facade is cut into a rose-red sandstone cliff.

editions.name: Hagia Sophia
editions.by: Isidore of Miletus and Anthemius of Tralles
editions.note: Built in under six years for Emperor Justinian. Its dome seems to float on a ring of windows.

editions.name: Angkor Wat
editions.note: The largest religious monument in the world, laid out as a model of the universe.

editions.name: Sainte-Chapelle
editions.note: Walls turned almost entirely into stained glass, 15 windows about 15 meters tall each.

editions.name: Alhambra
editions.note: Palaces of carved plaster, tile and running water, built by the last Muslim dynasty in Spain.

editions.name: Forbidden City
editions.note: Home to 24 emperors over almost 500 years, and one of the largest groups of wooden buildings in the world.

editions.name: Florence Cathedral dome
editions.note: Brunelleschi built the biggest dome of his time without wooden centering, laying the bricks in a herringbone pattern.

editions.name: Saint Basil's Cathedral
editions.note: Nine chapels under onion domes, built for Ivan the Terrible. The bright colors were painted later.

editions.name: Himeji Castle
editions.note: Called the White Heron for its white plaster walls. It came through wartime bombing and earthquakes almost untouched.

editions.name: Sheikh Lotfollah Mosque
editions.note: No minaret, no courtyard. Just a tiled dome whose color shifts from cream to pink through the day.

editions.name: Taj Mahal
editions.note: Shah Jahan built it as a tomb for his wife Mumtaz Mahal. White marble inlaid with semi-precious stones.

editions.name: Great Mosque of Djenné
editions.note: The largest mud-brick building in the world. The whole town re-plasters it every year in a festival.

editions.name: Eiffel Tower
editions.note: Built for the 1889 World's Fair and meant to come down after 20 years. Many Parisian artists petitioned against it.

editions.name: Sagrada Família
editions.note: Begun in 1882 and still being built. Gaudí worked on it for over 40 years and is buried in its crypt.

editions.name: Secession Building
editions.note: Built for Vienna's breakaway artists. Locals nicknamed its dome of 3,000 gilded laurel leaves the golden cabbage.

editions.name: Casa Milà
editions.note: Locals called it La Pedrera, the stone quarry. The chimneys on the roof look like helmeted warriors.

editions.name: Chrysler Building
editions.note: Its spire was built in secret inside the crown, then raised in about 90 minutes to beat a rival to world's tallest.

editions.name: Einstein Tower
editions.note: An observatory built to test the theory of relativity. Meant to be poured concrete, it's mostly brick plastered to look poured.

editions.name: Goetheanum
editions.note: Built after the wooden first one burned down. A huge sculpted concrete mass with hardly a right angle.

editions.name: Bauhaus Dessau
editions.note: The school building that defined the style, with a glass curtain wall wrapped around the workshops.

editions.name: Stockholm Public Library
editions.note: A cylinder on a box. Inside, the round hall is lined with books all the way around.

editions.name: Van Nelle Factory
editions.note: A coffee, tea and tobacco factory in glass so the workers had daylight. Le Corbusier called it the most beautiful spectacle of the modern age.

editions.name: Paimio Sanatorium
editions.note: A tuberculosis hospital designed around the patient, down to quiet sinks and ceilings colored for people lying in bed.

editions.name: Barcelona Pavilion
editions.by: Ludwig Mies van der Rohe and Lilly Reich
editions.note: Germany's pavilion for the 1929 World's Fair. Torn down after the fair and rebuilt on the same spot in 1986.

editions.name: Grundtvig's Church
editions.note: About six million yellow bricks, shaped like a giant church organ.

editions.name: Shukhov Tower
editions.note: A radio tower of straight steel bars arranged into curved, twisting hyperboloids. Light and very strong.

editions.name: Unité d'Habitation
editions.note: A vertical city of 337 apartments with a shopping street halfway up and a running track and pool on the roof.

editions.name: Notre-Dame du Haut
editions.note: A chapel with a roof like an upturned hull and thick walls pierced by small colored windows.

editions.name: Palace of Assembly
editions.note: The parliament of the new city of Chandigarh, with a huge curved portico and a cooling-tower shape rising through the roof.

editions.name: National Parliament House
editions.note: Concrete cut through with huge circles and triangles. Kahn died in 1974, before it was finished.

editions.name: Salk Institute
editions.note: Two rows of labs face a travertine courtyard split by a thin channel of water that points at the Pacific.

editions.name: Seagram Building
editions.note: Set back from Park Avenue behind an open plaza. The bronze beams on the facade are there for looks, not structure.

editions.name: Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum
editions.note: One continuous spiral ramp: take the elevator up and walk down through the show. Wright died months before it opened.

editions.name: TWA Flight Center
editions.note: A terminal at JFK shaped like a bird about to take off. It's a hotel now.

editions.name: Gateway Arch
editions.note: 192 meters tall and exactly as wide as it is tall. The tallest arch in the world.

editions.name: Montreal Biosphere
editions.note: The US pavilion at Expo 67, a geodesic sphere 76 meters across. Its acrylic skin burned off in 1976.

editions.name: Habitat 67
editions.note: 354 concrete boxes stacked so every apartment gets a garden on a neighbor's roof. It began as Safdie's master's thesis.

editions.name: Sydney Opera House
editions.note: Every shell is cut from the same sphere, which is how it got built. Utzon quit in 1966 and never saw it finished.

editions.name: Cathedral of Brasília
editions.note: Sixteen curved concrete columns rise like hands. You enter through a dark tunnel and come up into the light.
editions.credit: Tissiana de A. de Souza · CC BY-SA 4.0

editions.name: National Congress of Brazil
editions.note: Twin towers between two bowls, one facing up and one facing down: the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate.

editions.name: São Paulo Museum of Art
editions.note: The galleries hang from two red beams 74 meters long, leaving a public plaza underneath. Inside, paintings float on glass easels.

editions.name: SESC Pompéia
editions.note: An old drum factory turned leisure center. Concrete towers joined by bridges, windows like holes punched in the wall.

editions.name: National Library of Argentina
editions.by: Clorindo Testa, Francisco Bullrich and Alicia Cazzaniga
editions.note: Designed in 1961 and finished three decades later. The reading rooms ride high on four huge legs over the park.
editions.credit: Gobierno de la Ciudad de Buenos Aires · CC BY 2.5 ar

editions.name: Bank of London and South America
editions.note: Testa wrapped a downtown corner in a concrete shell and left the inside one tall open space.

editions.name: Torres del Parque
editions.note: Three brick towers that curve and step down around the bullring, as if grown from the hills behind.

editions.name: Church of Christ the Worker
editions.note: Walls and roof in waving brick. Dieste was an engineer who made brick do what concrete does.

editions.name: Los Manantiales
editions.note: A restaurant roof of intersecting saddle curves in concrete only about 4 cm thick.

editions.name: UNAM Central Library
editions.note: Four windowless walls covered in a mosaic of colored stones telling the history of Mexico.

editions.name: Torres de Satélite
editions.note: Five triangular towers in red, yellow, white and blue. Sculpture at the scale of the highway.

editions.name: University City of Caracas
editions.note: A campus with art built in. Calder's floating clouds fill the ceiling of the Aula Magna.

editions.name: National Art Schools
editions.by: Ricardo Porro, Vittorio Garatti and Roberto Gottardi
editions.note: Built on a golf course after the revolution, with domes of thin Catalan brick vaults. Left unfinished for decades.

editions.name: Museo Soumaya
editions.note: A twisted body clad in 16,000 aluminum hexagons, built for Carlos Slim's art collection.

editions.name: Nakagin Capsule Tower
editions.note: 140 capsule apartments bolted to two cores, meant to be swapped out. None ever were, and it came down in 2022.

editions.name: Yoyogi National Gymnasium
editions.note: Built for the 1964 Tokyo Olympics. The roof hangs from steel cables like a suspension bridge.

editions.name: Church of the Light
editions.note: A concrete box with a cross cut through the wall behind the altar. The light is the only decoration.

editions.name: 21st Century Museum of Contemporary Art
editions.note: A round glass building with no front or back, open to the city on every side.

editions.name: Teshima Art Museum
editions.note: A thin concrete shell like a drop of water, with two holes open to the sky. Inside: light, wind and beads of water on the floor.

editions.name: Rolex Learning Center
editions.note: One continuous floor that rises and dips like hills, with round patios cut through it.

editions.name: Lotus Temple
editions.note: A Bahá'í house of worship of 27 marble petals, open to people of every faith.

editions.name: Heritance Kandalama
editions.note: A hotel built along a cliff and left for the jungle to swallow.

editions.name: Petronas Towers
editions.note: Floor plans based on an eight-pointed Islamic star. The world's tallest buildings from 1998 to 2004.

editions.name: Marina Bay Sands
editions.note: Three towers holding up a long sky park with a pool on top.

editions.name: The Interlace
editions.note: 31 apartment blocks stacked like Jenga in a hexagonal weave, with gardens in the gaps.

editions.name: Ningbo Museum
editions.note: Walls built from bricks and tiles salvaged from demolished villages. Wang Shu won the Pritzker in 2012.

editions.name: Beijing National Stadium
editions.note: The Bird's Nest, a lattice of steel that looks random. Built for the 2008 Olympics with Ai Weiwei as artistic consultant.

editions.name: CCTV Headquarters
editions.note: Two leaning towers joined at the top by a 75-meter overhang. A loop instead of a skyscraper.

editions.name: Dongdaemun Design Plaza
editions.note: About 45,000 aluminum panels, nearly all different, wrapped around a design center.

editions.name: Heydar Aliyev Center
editions.note: One white surface that rises out of the plaza and folds into the building, with no hard edges anywhere.

editions.name: Burj Khalifa
editions.note: 828 meters, the tallest building in the world since 2010. Its plan is based on a desert flower.

editions.name: Louvre Abu Dhabi
editions.note: A dome of eight layers of patterned steel, so sunlight falls through it like light through palm leaves.

editions.name: Museum of Islamic Art
editions.note: Pei came out of retirement in his late 80s and found his model in a 13th-century fountain at a mosque in Cairo.

editions.name: Hassan II Mosque
editions.note: Built partly over the Atlantic, with a minaret over 200 meters tall and a roof that slides open.

editions.name: Gando Primary School
editions.note: Kéré's first building, for his own village: clay bricks made by the villagers under a floating roof that keeps classrooms cool. He won the Pritzker in 2022.

editions.name: Zeitz MOCAA
editions.note: An old grain silo carved out from inside. Its concrete tubes are cut into a cathedral-like atrium.

editions.name: Kenyatta International Convention Centre
editions.note: A round tower topped with a saucer, next to a hall roofed like a traditional hut.

editions.name: Hallgrímskirkja
editions.note: Stepped concrete wings inspired by the basalt columns that form when lava cools. It took 41 years to build.

editions.name: Oslo Opera House
editions.note: A sloping white marble roof you can walk straight up from the fjord, like a glacier.

editions.name: CopenHill
editions.note: A waste-to-energy plant with a ski slope on its roof.

editions.name: Therme Vals
editions.note: Baths built from 60,000 slabs of local quartzite, half buried in the mountain.

editions.name: Atomium
editions.by: André Waterkeyn, André and Jean Polak
editions.note: An iron crystal magnified 165 billion times, built for the 1958 World's Fair.

editions.name: Dancing House
editions.note: Nicknamed Fred and Ginger for its two towers leaning on each other like dancers.

editions.name: Hundertwasserhaus
editions.note: Public housing with uneven floors, trees growing out of the rooms and no two windows alike. Hundertwasser called the straight line godless.

editions.name: Bosco Verticale
editions.note: Two apartment towers with hundreds of trees on their balconies. Botanists picked the species for each side.

editions.name: Torre Velasca
editions.note: A modern tower with a medieval silhouette: the top floors jut out on struts like a castle keep.

editions.name: Brion Cemetery
editions.note: A family tomb and garden of stepped concrete, water and two interlocking circles. Scarpa is buried there too.

editions.name: Palazzetto dello Sport
editions.note: A ribbed concrete dome held up by Y-shaped struts, built for the 1960 Rome Olympics.

editions.name: Berliner Philharmonie
editions.note: The orchestra plays in the middle and the audience sits all around on terraces, like vineyards on a hill.

editions.name: Jewish Museum Berlin
editions.note: A zinc zigzag slashed with windows, with empty spaces inside, the voids, you can see but not enter.

editions.name: Elbphilharmonie
editions.note: A glass wave set on top of an old brick warehouse on the harbor. It opened seven years late and about ten times over budget.

editions.name: Guggenheim Museum Bilbao
editions.note: Titanium curves drawn with software from the aerospace industry. It turned a declining port city into a destination.

editions.name: Louvre Pyramid
editions.note: A new entrance for the Louvre. Parisians hated it at first, the way they once hated the Eiffel Tower.

editions.name: Centre Pompidou
editions.note: Built inside out and color coded: blue for air, green for water, yellow for electricity, red for moving people.

editions.name: Lloyd's building
editions.note: Stairs, lifts and pipes all on the outside, so the trading floor inside is one open space.

editions.name: 30 St Mary Axe
editions.note: The Gherkin. Its round shape eases the wind at street level, and spiraling gaps pull fresh air through it.

editions.name: Barbican Estate
editions.note: Built on land flattened in the Blitz: towers, terraces, lakes and an arts center, all in hammered concrete.

editions.name: Trellick Tower
editions.note: The lifts live in a separate tower, linked to the flats by a bridge every three floors.

editions.name: Boston City Hall
editions.note: Often voted one of the ugliest buildings in America, and defended by architects as one of its best.

editions.name: Geisel Library
editions.note: Concrete hands holding up stacks of glass floors. Named for Dr. Seuss, Theodor Geisel.

editions.name: Marina City
editions.note: Two corncob towers: parking spirals up the first 19 floors, apartments shaped like petals above.

editions.name: Thorncrown Chapel
editions.note: A glass chapel in the Ozark woods, built only from pieces small enough for two people to carry up the trail.

editions.name: La Muralla Roja
editions.note: Apartments stacked like a North African casbah on the cliffs, with stairs and courtyards in pink, red and blue.

editions.name: Leça Swimming Pools
editions.note: Concrete walls slipped between the rocks so the sea fills the pools. Siza was in his early thirties.

editions.name: Bank of Georgia headquarters
editions.note: Built for the Ministry of Highways: concrete blocks crossing like a highway interchange, leaving the ground open.

editions.name: Genex Tower
editions.note: Two towers joined at the top by a bridge and a round restaurant. Belgrade's gate from the airport.

editions.name: Kunsthaus Graz
editions.note: Locals call it the Friendly Alien. Its blue acrylic skin is fitted with rings of light that can show simple pictures at night.

editions.name: Kimbell Art Museum
editions.note: A row of long concrete vaults, each split along the top by a skylight. Curved aluminum reflectors spread the daylight across the ceilings.

editions.name: Phillips Exeter Academy Library
editions.note: Brick outside, concrete inside. The atrium walls are cut with giant circles that show every floor of books at once.

editions.name: Church of Saint Francis of Assisi
editions.note: Four concrete parabolas side by side, with a blue tile mural by Candido Portinari on the back. The Church refused to consecrate it until 1959.

editions.name: Flatiron Building
editions.note: A triangle on a triangular block where Broadway crosses Fifth Avenue. At its tip it's only about two meters wide.

editions.name: Empire State Building
editions.note: Built in about thirteen months. It was the tallest building in the world for almost forty years.

editions.name: Guaranty Building
editions.note: An early steel-frame skyscraper covered top to bottom in ornamented terracotta. Sullivan wrote "form ever follows function" the same year.

editions.name: Johnson Wax Headquarters
editions.note: The Great Workroom is a forest of slim "lily pad" columns. Inspectors doubted them, so Wright loaded a test column until it held about five times what it had to.

editions.name: Neue Nationalgalerie
editions.note: A black steel roof about 65 meters square, held up by just eight columns. The glass hall under it is almost empty on purpose.

editions.name: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library
editions.note: The walls are thin panels of marble with no windows. In daylight they glow amber inside and keep direct sun off the books.

editions.name: Breuer Building
editions.note: Built for the Whitney Museum as an upside-down ziggurat of dark granite, each floor reaching farther out over the sidewalk.

editions.name: Seattle Central Library
editions.note: Floors stacked off-kilter inside a diamond net of steel and glass. The Books Spiral runs the whole collection along one continuous ramp.

editions.name: Vitra Fire Station
editions.note: Zaha Hadid's first finished building: sharp concrete planes that look frozen mid-motion. It was a fire station for only a few years and now shows chairs.

editions.name: Royal National Theatre
editions.note: Layers of concrete terraces on the South Bank. You can still see the grain of the wooden molds in the walls.

editions.name: Isokon building
editions.note: Small concrete flats with built-in furniture, an early modernist experiment in London. Agatha Christie, Walter Gropius and Marcel Breuer all lived there.

editions.name: De La Warr Pavilion
editions.note: A seaside pavilion with a glass staircase that curves out toward the sea. One of the first welded steel-frame buildings in Britain.

editions.name: Glasgow School of Art
editions.note: Mackintosh's masterpiece, with huge studio windows facing north for steady light. Fires in 2014 and 2018 gutted the inside.

editions.name: Battersea Power Station
editions.note: A brick cathedral of a power plant with four white chimneys. Pink Floyd flew an inflatable pig between them for an album cover.

editions.name: Stoclet Palace
editions.note: A banker's mansion outlined in bronze trim like a drawing. The dining room has a mosaic frieze by Gustav Klimt.

editions.name: Hôtel Tassel
editions.note: Often called the first Art Nouveau building. Inside, iron columns, wall paintings and floor mosaics all twist into the same whiplash lines.

editions.name: Looshaus
editions.note: Its plain walls across from the Imperial Palace caused such a scandal that Loos added window boxes of flowers. People called it the house without eyebrows.

editions.name: Austrian Postal Savings Bank
editions.note: The marble panels are held on with aluminum-capped bolts, and the banking hall floor is glass to light the room below.

editions.name: Fagus Factory
editions.note: A factory for shoe lasts whose glass corners have no columns behind them. It's often called the first modernist building.

editions.name: Chilehaus
editions.note: Ten stories of dark brick with a corner as sharp as a ship's bow. Its owner made his fortune shipping saltpeter from Chile.

editions.name: Helsinki Central Station
editions.note: Clad in Finnish granite, with two pairs of giant stone men holding glowing globes beside the doors.

editions.name: Temppeliaukio Church
editions.note: Blasted into a granite outcrop and covered with a copper dome. The raw rock walls give it great acoustics for concerts.

editions.name: St. Peter's Church
editions.note: Lewerentz didn't let the builders cut a single brick. The windows are sheets of glass clipped to the outside, with no frames.

editions.name: Louisiana Museum of Modern Art
editions.note: Low white galleries strung through a park by the sea, linked by glass corridors. Named after the first owner's three wives, all called Louise.

editions.name: Bruder Klaus Field Chapel
editions.note: Local farmers poured concrete around a tent of 112 tree trunks, then burned the wood out, leaving a charred room open to the sky.

editions.name: Arab World Institute
editions.note: The south wall is a grid of metal panels with camera-like apertures, made to open and close with the light like a mashrabiya screen.

editions.name: Casa del Fascio
editions.note: Faced in white marble, exactly half as tall as it is wide. Built as a Fascist party office, it's a key work of Italian Rationalism.

editions.name: Pirelli Tower
editions.note: A slim tower with tapered ends, like a blade seen edge on. Pier Luigi Nervi engineered its concrete frame.

editions.name: Lingotto
editions.note: A Fiat car factory with a test track on the roof. Cars were built floor by floor on the way up, then driven around the top.

editions.name: San Cataldo Cemetery
editions.note: A terracotta-red cube with rows of square windows and no roof. Rossi called it a house of the dead.
editions.credit: Dage - Looking For Europe · CC BY 2.0

editions.name: City of Arts and Sciences
editions.note: White ribbed buildings in an old riverbed. The planetarium is shaped like a giant eye with a lid that opens and closes.

editions.name: Torres Blancas
editions.note: Round balconies grow off a concrete trunk like a tree. Despite the name, there's only one tower, and it isn't white.

editions.name: Palau de la Música Catalana
editions.note: A concert hall with walls of glass and a stained-glass skylight that hangs down into the room like an upside-down sun.

editions.name: Metropol Parasol
editions.note: Six giant timber mushrooms over a square in Seville, with a walkway along the top. Locals call it Las Setas, the mushrooms.

editions.name: Harpa
editions.by: Henning Larsen Architects with Olafur Eliasson
editions.note: A concert hall on the harbor wrapped in glass bricks by Olafur Eliasson, based on Iceland's basalt columns.

editions.name: Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum
editions.note: Raised on concrete pillars at the end of the Peace Park, lined up with the cenotaph and the ruined A-Bomb Dome.

editions.name: Sendai Mediatheque
editions.note: A glass box held up by thirteen hollow tubes of twisted steel that rise through every floor like seaweed.

editions.name: Kinkaku-ji
editions.note: A retirement villa turned Zen temple, its top two floors covered in gold leaf. A monk burned it down in 1950; what stands today was rebuilt in 1955.

editions.name: Jantar Mantar
editions.note: An observatory of giant stone instruments. Its sundial is about 27 meters tall and tells local time to within a couple of seconds.

editions.name: Chand Baori
editions.note: A stepwell thirteen stories deep, with about 3,500 narrow steps zigzagging down to the water. The bottom stays several degrees cooler.

editions.name: Humayun's Tomb
editions.note: The first great garden tomb in India, red sandstone and white marble in the middle of a four-part garden. It inspired the Taj Mahal.

editions.name: Azadi Tower
editions.note: A gateway clad in about 8,000 blocks of white marble. Amanat was 24 when he won the competition to design it.

editions.name: Süleymaniye Mosque
editions.note: Sinan's great mosque for Suleiman the Magnificent. Soot from its oil lamps was drawn into one room and collected to make ink.

editions.name: Kuwait Towers
editions.note: Three needles on the waterfront, two carrying spheres covered in blue, green and gray enamel discs. They hold water tanks and a restaurant.

editions.name: HSBC Main Building
editions.note: The floors hang from steel masts on the outside, so every level is open. A mirrored sunscoop bounces daylight down into the atrium.

editions.name: Potala Palace
editions.note: Thirteen stories climbing a hill in Lhasa at about 3,700 meters. The White Palace went up in the 1640s, the Red Palace in the 1690s.

editions.name: Temple of Heaven
editions.note: Three tiers of blue roof, the color of heaven. The round hall you see was rebuilt after lightning burned it down in 1889.

editions.name: Chengqi Lou
editions.note: The king of the tulou: a round earth fortress with four rings and about 400 rooms, built for one Hakka clan.

editions.name: Borobudur
editions.note: The world's largest Buddhist temple: nine stacked platforms and 504 Buddhas, many sitting inside stone bells with lattice walls.

editions.name: Bulguksa
editions.note: A temple on stone terraces, reached by stone staircases called the Blue Cloud and White Cloud Bridges.

editions.name: Taipei 101
editions.note: Shaped like a stalk of bamboo in eight segments. A 660-tonne steel ball hangs near the top to calm the sway in typhoons.

editions.name: Church of Saint George
editions.note: Carved downward out of solid rock in the shape of a cross. Its roof is level with the ground around it.

editions.name: Eastgate Centre
editions.note: Offices with no conventional air conditioning. Like a termite mound, it pulls in cool night air and lets warm air out through its chimneys.

editions.name: Basilica of Our Lady of Peace
editions.note: Modeled on St. Peter's in Rome, it's listed as the largest church in the world. Built between 1985 and 1989.

editions.name: Cairo Tower
editions.note: A 187-meter concrete tower with a lattice skin shaped like a lotus. For a decade it was the tallest structure in Africa.

editions.name: Bibliotheca Alexandrina
editions.note: A tilted disc like a sun rising from the sea, near where the ancient Library of Alexandria stood. Its granite wall is carved with letters from scripts around the world.

editions.name: National Theatre of Nigeria
editions.note: Built for FESTAC 77, the festival of Black and African arts. People compare its shape to a general's cap.

editions.name: Smiling Lion
editions.note: An apartment block in Maputo with a face: its jagged balconies and window frames grin like a row of teeth.

editions.name: National Museum of Anthropology
editions.note: The courtyard is sheltered by "the umbrella", a huge concrete roof on a single bronze-clad column, with water pouring down around it.

editions.name: El Castillo
editions.note: 91 steps on each side plus the top platform make 365. At the equinoxes, shadows make a serpent slide down the north stairs.

editions.name: Teatro Colón
editions.by: Francesco Tamburini, Vittorio Meano and Jules Dormal
editions.note: A horseshoe opera house with some of the best acoustics in the world. It took three architects and twenty years to build.

editions.name: Palacio Barolo
editions.note: An office tower laid out after Dante's Divine Comedy: hell at the bottom, purgatory in the middle, heaven in the lighthouse on top.

editions.name: Narkomfin Building
editions.note: An experiment in shared living: small flats linked by a bridge to a common kitchen, gym and laundry. Restored in 2020 after decades of decay.

editions.name: Ještěd Tower
editions.note: A hotel and TV tower on a mountaintop, shaped so it carries the line of the peak up into the sky.

editions.name: Slovak Radio Building
editions.by: Štefan Svetko, Štefan Ďurkovič and Barnabáš Kissling
editions.note: An upside-down pyramid of rust-brown steel, with the concert hall tucked underneath.

editions.name: Palace of Culture and Science
editions.note: A gift from the Soviet Union. The joke goes that the best view of Warsaw is from its terrace, the one place you can't see it.

editions.name: Munich Olympic Stadium
editions.note: Its tent roof of clear acrylic hangs from nets of steel cable, light and open on purpose, a world away from the 1936 Games.

editions.name: Grande Arche
editions.note: A hollow cube about 110 meters across, lined up with the Arc de Triomphe and the Louvre. Notre-Dame could fit in the opening.

editions.name: Centre Pompidou-Metz
editions.by: Shigeru Ban and Jean de Gastines
editions.note: A woven timber roof like a giant hat, inspired by a Chinese woven bamboo hat Ban found in Paris.

editions.name: Cube Houses
editions.note: Yellow cubes tipped 45 degrees on poles, each one a home. Blom thought of each cube as a tree and the whole row as a forest.

editions.name: Zonnestraal
editions.note: A tuberculosis sanatorium of thin white concrete and glass, for light and air. Duiker meant it to last only as long as TB did.

editions.name: Aqua Tower
editions.note: 82 stories where every balcony is a slightly different shape, so the tower ripples like water.

editions.name: The Sea Ranch
editions.note: Shed-roofed wooden houses on the cliffs, angled to shrug off the wind. The redwood was left to weather gray like the old barns nearby.

editions.name: Burj Al Arab
editions.note: A hotel shaped like the sail of a dhow, on its own man-made island. The white sail is a screen of coated glass-fiber fabric.

editions.name: Toronto City Hall
editions.note: Two curved towers of different heights wrap around a saucer-shaped council chamber. Revell called it the Eye of Government.

editions.name: Parthenon
editions.note: It looks perfectly straight, but almost nothing is: the floor bulges upward and the columns lean slightly inward to fool the eye.

editions.name: Lovell Beach House
editions.note: Raised on five concrete frames, so the beach runs right underneath the house.

editions.name: Lovell Health House
editions.note: The first steel-frame house in the United States, for a health guru who believed in sun and fresh air. The frame went up in about forty hours.

editions.name: Dymaxion House
editions.note: A round aluminum house hung from a central mast, made to be built in an aircraft factory and shipped in a tube. Only two prototypes were built.

editions.name: Villa Noailles
editions.note: A cubist villa for the art patrons Charles and Marie-Laure de Noailles. Man Ray shot a film there, and it now hosts a design festival.

editions.name: Villa Girasole
editions.note: A house that follows the sun. The upper floor turns on circular tracks, one full turn in about nine hours.

editions.name: Sir John Soane's Museum
editions.note: An architect's home packed with antiquities, mirrors and skylights. By law it has been kept the way he left it in 1837.

editions.name: Strawberry Hill House
editions.note: Horace Walpole's white Gothic fantasy, which helped start the Gothic Revival. He wrote the first Gothic novel there.

editions.name: Monticello
editions.note: Jefferson designed and redesigned his own house for about forty years. It's on the back of the US nickel.

editions.name: Hvitträsk
editions.by: Herman Gesellius, Armas Lindgren and Eliel Saarinen
editions.note: A shared home and studio for three young architects, built of logs and stone on a lake shore like a castle from a folk tale.

editions.name: Glaumbær
editions.note: A farm of turf houses joined by passages, the walls stacked from sod and stone to keep the warmth in. People lived there until 1947.

editions.name: Gasshō-zukuri farmhouses
editions.note: Steep thatched roofs shaped like hands pressed together in prayer, built to shed heavy snow. Silkworms were raised in the attics.

editions.name: Trulli
editions.note: Whitewashed houses with cone roofs of stacked stone and no mortar. Legend says owners could pull the roof down when the tax man came.

editions.name: Tongkonan
editions.note: Ancestral houses on stilts with roofs that sweep up like buffalo horns or the bow of a boat. The walls are carved and painted red, black and white.

editions.name: Musgum huts
editions.note: Tall shell-shaped huts of sun-dried mud. The raised patterns on the outside double as footholds for climbing up to repair them.

editions.name: Hanging Houses
editions.note: Houses built out over the edge of a gorge, their wooden balconies hanging above the drop. One holds a museum of Spanish abstract art.

editions.name: Haus am Horn
editions.note: The first Bauhaus house, built for the school's 1923 show: a tall living room in the middle and smaller rooms all around it.

editions.name: Eames Lounge Chair
editions.note: Charles wanted it to look like "a well-used first baseman's mitt". It made its debut on live American TV.

editions.name: Cab
editions.note: A steel frame dressed in a leather skin that zips up the inside of each leg, like a fitted coat.

editions.name: Savonarola chair
editions.note: A folding chair made of interlocking curved slats, later named after the Florentine friar Girolamo Savonarola.

editions.name: Chippendale chair
editions.note: Carved mahogany with a pierced back and claw-and-ball feet. Chippendale's 1754 pattern book spread the look across Britain and America.

editions.name: Akan stool
editions.note: Carved from one block of wood. For the Akan, a stool holds its owner's soul, and the Golden Stool is the throne of the Asante.

editions.name: Safari Chair
editions.note: Based on a chair used by British officers in India. It comes apart without tools so it can be carried anywhere.

editions.name: Domus chair
editions.note: Designed for a student housing building in Helsinki, it became one of the first Finnish chairs sold around the world.

editions.name: S-Chair
editions.note: A single S-shaped curve on a round base, first made of welded steel wrapped in woven rush.

editions.name: Bent plywood armchair
editions.note: Cut and bent from a single sheet of plywood, with no joints at all. It was meant for hot climates, where glue and screws can fail.

editions.name: Thonet rocking chair
editions.note: Thonet made the first bentwood rocking chair in 1860: loops and spirals of steam-bent beech around a caned seat.

editions.name: Lamino
editions.note: Laminated wood and a sheepskin seat. It was voted Sweden's best furniture design of the 20th century.

editions.name: Ekstrem
editions.note: A tangle of padded tubes that lets you sit any way you like: sideways, backwards or curled up.

editions.name: Tripp Trapp
editions.note: A wooden high chair that grows with the child: the seat and footrest move up and down, so it lasts from toddler to adult.

editions.name: Spaghetti chair
editions.note: A thin steel frame strung with colored PVC cord, like strands of spaghetti.

editions.name: AJ lamp
editions.note: Designed for the SAS Royal Hotel in Copenhagen. A slanted shade on a thin stand, with a round hole cut in the base.

editions.name: Lava lamp
editions.note: Walker got the idea from a homemade egg timer he saw in a pub: blobs of colored wax rise and sink in warm liquid.

editions.name: Murano chandelier
editions.note: Blown glass arms, leaves and flowers in pastel colors, a style called ciocca, a bouquet.

editions.name: Gallé lamp
editions.note: Layered cameo glass, carved and etched into flowers and leaves that glow when the lamp is lit.

editions.name: Bocca sofa
editions.note: A sofa shaped like big red lips, a nod to Salvador Dalí's Mae West Lips Sofa from the 1930s.

editions.name: Pratone
editions.by: Giorgio Ceretti, Pietro Derossi and Riccardo Rosso
editions.note: A giant patch of green foam grass blades to lounge in. The blades bend and spring back.

editions.name: Billy bookcase
editions.note: A plain flat-pack bookcase sold by the tens of millions. Lundgren is also credited with IKEA's flat pack: he took the legs off a table to fit it in a car.

editions.name: Boulle cabinet
editions.note: Cabinetmaker to Louis XIV. His marquetry of brass and tortoiseshell was so famous it's still called boulle work.

editions.name: Arabesque table
editions.note: A low table of bent plywood curling into an open S under a free-form glass top.

editions.name: Bauhaus cradle
editions.note: A cradle built from a triangle, a square and a circle, painted in Kandinsky's colors: yellow, red and blue.

editions.name: Berlin chair
editions.note: Flat boards in black, white and grays, put together so no two sides match. Made for a model room at a 1923 exhibition in Berlin.

editions.name: Drouant side chair
editions.note: Made for the Restaurant Drouant in Paris, where the Goncourt Prize is awarded. Ruhlmann was the great name of Art Deco luxury.

editions.name: Fauteuil à la reine
editions.note: Gilded carving and a flat upholstered back. Georges Jacob made chairs like this for Marie Antoinette's rooms at Versailles.

editions.name: Hitchcock chair
editions.note: One of the first American chairs made in a factory, from parts cut in bulk. Painted black with stenciled gold fruit and flowers.

editions.name: Roman oil lamp
editions.note: Pressed from molds by the millions across the Roman Empire. Olive oil went in the hole on top, and a wick burned at the nozzle.

editions.name: Carimate
editions.note: Designed for a golf club in Carimate, near Milan: a country chair lacquered bright red, with a woven rush seat.

editions.name: GJ chair
editions.note: Two sheets of molded plywood folded like paper. It won a big furniture competition in 1963, but only about 300 were made at the time.

editions.name: Ultrafragola
editions.note: A tall mirror in a wavy frame of plastic that glows pink from inside. The name means super strawberry.

editions.name: Bone Chair
editions.note: Shaped by software that copies how bones grow: material where the chair takes weight, none where it doesn't. Cast in one piece of aluminum.
